title: WIHIC | Give each person useful work to do

qcReview.basis: Eight English items 41–48 and the five frequency choices match Fraser (2023), Appendix A Table A1. The appendix’s top answer is Almost Always. Source © Fraser 2023, CC BY 4.0. The project retains C and the eight-item complete-response mean (1–5), without thresholds. This version adds original feedback only, for the student who answered.

interpretations.headline: Give each person useful work to do
interpretations.summary:
Four students have one set of materials and several ideas. One explains the starting plan, a second checks the evidence, a third tries another approach, and a fourth helps compare their results. They change jobs on the next round. That makes it easier for everyone to help shape the answer.

Your answers describe how often you worked with classmates, shared materials, and learned from one another in this class. A group’s chance to work well can depend on how the task is set up and whether everyone can take a turn. Use the report to spot one way to make shared work feel more shared.

guidance.text: At the start of a group task, agree on the goal and divide the first jobs. Pause midway so everyone can say what they found. Swap one role if a person hasn’t had a useful turn yet.
At the end, ask each person to name one thing they learned from someone else. Pick one arrangement your group could keep next time.

limitations: © Barry J. Fraser, 2023. Adapted from What Is Happening In this Class? (WIHIC), Appendix A, Table A1, in The Evolution of the Field of Learning Environments Research, Education Sciences, 13(3), 257. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci13030257 (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The project presents one part separately, with its own instruction, scoring of complete answers, and student feedback.
The result is the mean of eight answers about one class. The five original answer choices run from Almost Never (1) to Almost Always (5). If an answer is missing, this part has no score.

Using this separate eight-question form with English-reading students ages 12–15 in grades 7–9 is this project’s scope. This item set has no separate validation or group benchmark. Each part of WIHIC stands alone in the report.
report.disclaimer: This report describes your experience in one class. It is for reflection and does not grade you, your classmates, or your teacher.
